During the parent interview, Sofía’s mother reported that Sofía lives with her, her 6-year-old brother and her maternal grandmother. Her mother works, and her grandmother cares for both children after school. Her mother reported that Sofía’s father lives in another state and has no regular contact with her. Her mother completed the interview in English and reported that her grandmother speaks only Spanish. Her mother’s first priority is for Sofía to stop hurting her brother. She also wants Sofía to calm down without breaking things, leave for school without a struggle, develop a friendship and shower independently.

According to the Comprehensive Diagnostic Evaluation (CDE), the evaluating psychologist diagnosed Autism Spectrum Disorder, without accompanying intellectual impairment, with accompanying language impairment in pragmatic language, and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, combined presentation. The CDE identified the psychiatrist as the prescriber of methylphenidate extended release, 18 mg every morning. Sofía’s mother reported that Sofía began taking the medication in March 2026 and sees the psychiatrist every 6 weeks. Her mother described better attention in the morning but reported that afternoon outbursts are worse than before. Regarding birth history, her mother reported that Sofía was born at 39 weeks without complications.

Sofía’s mother reported that early developmental milestones occurred on time and that Sofía spoke in sentences by age 2. According to her mother, teachers first raised concerns in kindergarten about outbursts and Sofía playing alone. The CDE described difficulty sustaining a conversation despite her ability to speak in complete sentences. The evaluating psychologist noted that Sofía talks at length about train schedules without asking the other person questions and does not clarify what she means when someone misunderstands her.

According to her mother, Sofía attends 4th grade at Ejemplo Elementary School from 8:30 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in a general education classroom with exceptional student education support. Her Individualized Education Program (IEP) describes grade-level reading, with strengths in decoding and vocabulary. The IEP places her math performance about 1 year below grade level and notes that she does not finish independent work. The IEP provides 300 minutes per week of specialized instruction in the general education classroom, 60 minutes per week of speech-language therapy for pragmatic language and 30 minutes per week of school counseling. Its accommodations include a visual schedule, a break card, advance warning before transitions, seating away from the door, extended time on assignments and headphones in the cafeteria. The IEP targets using the break card instead of leaving class, taking conversational turns on a peer’s topic and using a calming strategy when frustrated. The IEP does not include behavior analysis services, and her mother reported during follow-up that the school-based functional behavior assessment remains pending. Her mother reported no previous applied behavior analysis and no improvement during an earlier 6-month period of school counseling. The CDE recommended a social skills group in addition to continued school speech-language services and medication management.

At home, Sofía’s mother reported that Sofía hits, kicks or pushes her brother during disputes over the tablet or television remote. She also described threats, torn homework and biting of the hand or wrist when Sofía is frustrated. Her mother reported that Sofía once struck her head against the bedroom wall and received urgent care for a cut above her eyebrow; the urgent care record was not available. Her mother described repeated prompting to start a shower and said Sofía does not wash her hair independently. Although Sofía dresses herself, her mother reported that she becomes distressed when her preferred outfits are in the wash. On school mornings, her mother reported that Sofía sometimes locks herself in the bathroom or refuses to board the bus. At school, the IEP documents leaving the classroom during writing or group work and pushing or kicking peers at lunch and recess. In the community, her mother reported that Sofía runs across streets without looking and cannot yet order food or pay for a purchase on her own.

Sofía’s mother described her as affectionate with her grandmother and said she helps feed the family dog, enjoys drawing maps and reads books about trains. Her mother reported that Sofía usually plays alone on the tablet and has no friends at school or in the neighborhood. During the summer program, the evaluating psychologist observed Sofía playing alone during free time and talking to an adult about train schedules without checking the adult’s interest. The CDE also described Sofía covering her ears and leaving the room in the cafeteria and during assemblies. Her mother reported that changes to the evening routine can lead to screaming and that Sofía may refuse to get out of the car when the route home changes.

The clinical need for applied behavior analysis (ABA) is supported by the Comprehensive Diagnostic Evaluation (CDE), Sofía’s Individualized Education Program (IEP), the parent interview and direct observation at home, at the public library and at the neighborhood park. Her mother was the respondent for the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Third Edition (Vineland-3) Comprehensive Parent/Caregiver Interview Form and the BASC-3 Parenting Relationship Questionnaire (PRQ). In the CDE, the evaluating psychologist diagnosed Autism Spectrum Disorder, without accompanying intellectual impairment, with accompanying language impairment in pragmatic language, and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, combined presentation. These sources show deficits in self-care and daily living, communication, coping with change and demands, safety, and participation with peers and in the community.

On the Vineland-3, Sofía’s Adaptive Behavior Composite standard score of 74 was Moderately Low, at the 4th percentile. About 4 in 100 children her age scored this low or lower in everyday functioning. Socialization was her lowest domain, with a standard score of 66 at the 1st percentile, in the Low range. Coping was her lowest subdomain v-scale score at 5; Interpersonal Relationships at 7 and Play and Leisure at 9 were also Low. Her mother described the daily impact: a change in the route home can keep Sofía from getting out of the car, and she has no friends in the neighborhood. Daily Living Skills, with a standard score of 72 at the 3rd percentile, was Moderately Low. Community and Domestic v-scale scores of 8 and 9 were Low, while Personal at 10 was Moderately Low, consistent with her mother’s report that Sofía needs help making purchases and showering. Communication was Moderately Low, with a standard score of 81 at the 10th percentile. Written and Receptive v-scale scores of 11 and 12 were Moderately Low, while Expressive at 13 was Adequate. As the IEP describes, Sofía can form complete sentences but has difficulty understanding nonliteral language. Motor Skills was a relative strength, with an Adequate standard score of 88 at the 21st percentile; Gross Motor at 14 was Adequate, while Fine Motor at 12 was Moderately Low. On the Vineland-3, the Maladaptive Behavior Index and Externalizing v-scale scores were both 22, Clinically Significant; Internalizing at 19 was Elevated. Her mother rated hitting, kicking or pushing others, intentionally damaging her own or others’ property, threatening harm to others and refusing school as occurring often. She also endorsed biting herself or banging her head, with a rating of 1 rather than the rating of 2 for often.

In self-care, Sofía’s mother identified independent showering as a priority. During direct observation of the evening routine at home, Sofía needed 14 verbal prompts over 38 minutes before she entered the shower and did not wash her hair. Even sustained adult prompting got her into the shower without completing the routine. ABA will address starting the shower with fewer prompts and washing her hair independently.

In communication, Sofía’s difficulty is sustaining an exchange, not finding words to describe a preferred subject. During direct observation at home, she spoke about train schedules for 11 minutes without pausing and did not respond to 2 attempts to change the topic. The IEP describes similar difficulty taking turns in classroom conversations. Sofía needs to learn to respond to another person’s contribution and take a turn on a topic she did not choose.

Changes and demands interrupt both homework and family outings. During direct observation at the library, Sofía sat on the floor and screamed for 9 minutes when her mother told her it was time to leave the train section. A staff member asked her mother to take her outside. Across home and community observations, Verbal outbursts occurred 6 times in 6 hours and lasted 6 to 15 minutes, delaying tasks and transitions. Her mother reported that the family drops homework after outbursts, and the IEP describes almost daily outbursts when tasks change or Sofía loses a game. Consistent with these accounts, the BCBA identified escape from demands and transitions as maintaining Verbal outbursts. Sofía needs to learn to request a break or help and resume an activity after a change, in keeping with her mother’s priority for her to calm down without Property destruction.

Physical aggression places Sofía’s brother at risk of injury, her mother’s first concern. Her mother reported a bruise on his upper arm and described several episodes per day, usually over the tablet or television remote. Direct observation documented 6 episodes in 6 hours, including at the park, where Sofía pushed her brother off a swing when he did not get off immediately. The IEP reports about 2 physical altercations per week with peers, mainly at lunch and recess. The BCBA identified escape from demands as the primary maintaining consequence and access to preferred items as secondary. Sofía needs to manage demands and wait for access without hitting, kicking or pushing. Hand biting (self-injury) is an additional safety target.

Leaving the area and school refusal limits attendance and creates immediate danger in the community. During direct observation on the way to the park, Sofía pulled free of her mother’s hand and ran across the street without looking. There was no traffic at that moment, but she crossed without checking. At school, the IEP documents departures from class 2 to 4 times per week, usually during writing or group work. Her mother reported refusal on 6 of 20 school days; on those mornings, her mother was late to work or Sofía stayed home with her grandmother. The BCBA identified escape from academic and social demands as maintaining this behavior. ABA will address leaving home for school and crossing streets safely with an adult.

Peer participation breaks down even when another child initiates play. During direct observation at the park, 2 girls invited Sofía to play tag. Sofía recited a bus schedule, the girls walked away and she played alone. The evaluating psychologist also documented solitary play during free time at the school summer program. Responding to an invitation and joining a shared activity are skills Sofía needs to develop the friendship her mother wants for her.

Direct observation showed that the demands of each setting mattered. At home, neither homework attempt ended in completed work; after the first, her grandmother gave Sofía the tablet. At the library and park, social opportunities and transitions remained difficult even without homework demands. District approval for school observation by the BCBA was pending; school evidence comes from the IEP and the evaluating psychologist’s summer program observation.

These findings establish the medical necessity of individualized ABA at home for school departure, hygiene and safe family routines, and in the community for street safety, transitions and peer participation. Teaching will match skills to what each behavior allows Sofía to obtain or avoid. Her mother’s BASC-3 PRQ responses indicated low parenting confidence and heightened relational frustration, consistent with her report that she has begun avoiding outings. Training will help her mother and grandmother support these skills in the routines they manage. ABA will complement school instruction, pragmatic language therapy and counseling by addressing daily functioning outside the classroom; it will not duplicate academic instruction or psychiatric medication management. The BCBA will measure progress through direct data on target behaviors, prompts needed for self-care, independent responses during transitions and participation in community activities, along with the Vineland-3 and BASC-3 PRQ at reassessment.

The need for applied behavior analysis (ABA) was assessed through the Comprehensive Diagnostic Evaluation (CDE), Sofía’s Individualized Education Program (IEP), interviews with her mother and direct observation at home, at the public library and at the neighborhood park. Her mother was the respondent for the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Third Edition (Vineland-3) Comprehensive Parent/Caregiver Interview Form and the BASC-3 Parenting Relationship Questionnaire (PRQ). In the CDE, the evaluating psychologist diagnosed Autism Spectrum Disorder, without accompanying intellectual impairment, with accompanying language impairment in pragmatic language, and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, combined presentation. Together, these sources identify deficits in self-care and daily living, communication, coping with change and demands, safety, and participation with peers and in the community.

On the Vineland-3, Sofía’s Adaptive Behavior Composite standard score of 74 was Moderately Low, at the 4th percentile, indicating less independence in everyday activities than most children her age. Socialization was her lowest domain, with a standard score of 66 (Low, 1st percentile). Within Socialization, her lowest v-scale score was in Coping (5), followed by Interpersonal Relationships (7) and Play and Leisure (9), all Low. Her mother described difficulty with even a change in the route home and reported that Sofía has no friends at school or in the neighborhood. Her Daily Living Skills standard score of 72 (Moderately Low, 3rd percentile) reflects dependence on adults at home and on outings. Community (8) and Domestic (9) were Low; Personal (10) was Moderately Low, consistent with her mother’s report that Sofía dresses herself but needs help with hygiene. Her Communication standard score was 81 (Moderately Low, 10th percentile). Receptive (12) and Written (11) were Moderately Low, while Expressive (13) was Adequate. As the IEP describes, Sofía can speak in complete sentences but has difficulty understanding nonliteral language. Motor Skills was a relative strength, with a standard score of 88 (Adequate, 21st percentile); Gross Motor was Adequate (14), while Fine Motor was Moderately Low (12). On the Vineland-3 Maladaptive Behavior domain, Internalizing was Elevated (19), while Externalizing and the Maladaptive Behavior Index were both Clinically Significant (22). On the critical items, her mother rated hitting, kicking or pushing others, intentionally damaging property, threatening to hurt others and refusing school as occurring often. She also endorsed biting herself or banging her head at a rating of 1. These concerns extend beyond distress: her mother reported injury to Sofía’s brother and missed school days.

In self-care, Sofía depends on an adult to start her shower and does not complete hair washing independently. During direct observation of the evening routine at home, Sofía needed 14 verbal prompts over 38 minutes before she entered the shower. Even after that sustained assistance, she did not wash her hair. Her mother identified independent bathing as a priority. ABA will address starting the shower with fewer reminders and completing hygiene tasks without an adult directing each step.

In communication, Sofía’s ability to speak at length does not translate into a reciprocal exchange. During direct observation at home, she spoke about train schedules for 11 minutes without responding to 2 attempts to change the topic. The CDE described difficulty recognizing misunderstandings, and the IEP documented difficulty taking conversational turns. Sofía needs to learn to respond to another person’s contribution and sustain an exchange on a topic she did not choose.

Difficulty coping with change and demands limits Sofía’s access to instruction. Her mother reported that when Sofía locked herself in the bathroom or would not board the bus, her grandmother sometimes kept her home. Her mother reported school refusal on 6 of 20 school days. Even when Sofía attends, the IEP documents that she leaves class 2 to 4 times per week, usually during writing or group work. The BCBA’s behavior assessment identifies escape from academic and social demands as maintaining Leaving the area and school refusal. Sofía needs to learn to tolerate changes in the school-morning routine, communicate when she needs help or a break and return to tasks. At home, the BCBA also identified Verbal outbursts, Property destruction and Hand biting (self-injury) as treatment targets.

Physical aggression places Sofía’s brother at risk during ordinary activities they share. Her mother reported several episodes per day, mostly over the tablet or television remote, and described a bruise on his upper arm. During direct observation, Sofía pushed her brother to the floor and kicked his leg after he picked up her train book. Across home and community observations, 6 episodes in 6 hours showed that the risk was not confined to one disagreement. The IEP also documents about 2 physical altercations per week, mostly at lunch and recess. The BCBA’s behavior assessment identifies escape from demands as the primary maintaining consequence and access to preferred items as secondary. Consistent with her mother’s first priority, Sofía needs to learn to cope with demands and share access to preferred materials without hurting another person.

Difficulty responding to peers limits Sofía’s participation even when other children initiate play. During direct observation at the park, 2 girls invited Sofía to play tag. She responded by reciting a bus schedule; the girls walked away, and Sofía played alone. The evaluating psychologist likewise documented solitary play during free time at the school summer program. To work toward the friendship her mother wants for her, Sofía needs to learn to recognize an invitation, respond to the activity a peer proposes and join the game.

Direct observation showed how quickly access to learning and community activities can be lost. At home, Sofía completed neither of 2 homework attempts. During the first, she tore the worksheet and screamed; her grandmother gave her the tablet, and she calmed within 2 minutes without completing the work. At the library, Sofía screamed for 9 minutes when it was time to leave, until a staff member asked her mother to take her outside. On the way to the park, Sofía pulled free and ran across the street without looking. Direct observation thus confirmed her mother’s concern that Sofía does not cross safely even with an adult beside her. School findings come from the IEP and the evaluating psychologist’s summer-program observation; district approval for the BCBA’s school observation was pending.

These findings establish the medical necessity of individualized ABA at home, where hygiene, homework and school departures are disrupted, and in the community, where street crossing and peer play require practice. ABA will address independence in these routines and teach skills matched to what maintains each behavior. Her mother’s BASC-3 PRQ responses indicated reduced parenting confidence and increased relational frustration. Training her mother and grandmother to support the same skills during daily routines will address the difficulties they face when demands or transitions lead to unsafe behavior. This work complements the IEP’s specialized instruction, pragmatic speech-language therapy and counseling by addressing behavior during family routines and outings; it does not replace classroom instruction, speech-language services, counseling or psychiatric medication management. Progress will be measured through direct data on target behaviors and skills, including prompts needed for showering, independent responses to peers and safe street crossings, and through the Vineland-3 and BASC-3 PRQ at reassessment.

According to the Comprehensive Diagnostic Evaluation (CDE), the evaluating psychologist diagnosed Sofía with Autism Spectrum Disorder, without accompanying intellectual impairment, with accompanying language impairment in pragmatic language, and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, combined presentation. Her mother completed the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Third Edition (Vineland-3) Comprehensive Parent/Caregiver Interview Form and the BASC-3 Parenting Relationship Questionnaire (PRQ). The parent interview, direct observation at home, at the public library and at the neighborhood park, and the school’s Individual Education Plan (IEP) provided evidence of how Sofía functions in daily routines. Together, these sources establish a need for applied behavior analysis (ABA) in self-care and daily living, communication, coping with changes and demands, safety, and participation with peers and in the community.

On the Vineland-3, Sofía’s Adaptive Behavior Composite standard score of 74 was Moderately Low, at the 4th percentile. About 4 in 100 children her age scored this low or lower in everyday independence. Socialization was her lowest domain, with a standard score of 66, Low, at the 1st percentile. Coping was her lowest subdomain (v-scale score 5, Low), consistent with her mother’s report that even a change in the route home can prevent Sofía from getting out of the car. Interpersonal Relationships (7) and Play and Leisure (9) were also Low; her mother described solitary play and no friendships. Daily Living Skills fell at the 3rd percentile (standard score 72, Moderately Low). Her Personal v-scale score of 10 was Moderately Low, consistent with dependence on reminders for hygiene. Domestic (9) and Community (8) were Low; although her mother reported that Sofía helps feed the dog, she cannot yet order food or pay at a store. Communication fell at the 10th percentile (standard score 81, Moderately Low). Receptive (12) and Written (11) were Moderately Low, while Expressive (13) was Adequate, consistent with the IEP’s description of complete sentences but difficulty understanding nonliteral language. Motor Skills were a relative strength (standard score 88, 21st percentile, Adequate), with stronger Gross Motor skills (14, Adequate) than Fine Motor skills (12, Moderately Low). On the Maladaptive Behavior domain, Internalizing was Elevated (v-scale score 19), while Externalizing and the Maladaptive Behavior Index were both Clinically Significant (v-scale score 22 each). Her mother rated hitting, kicking or pushing others, deliberately damaging property, threatening to hurt others and refusing school as occurring often. She also endorsed self-biting or head banging at a rating of 1.

In self-care, Sofía can dress herself, according to her mother, but does not complete bathing with comparable independence. During direct observation of the evening routine at home, Sofía needed 14 verbal prompts over 38 minutes before she entered the shower. She did not wash her hair. The difficulty extends beyond starting a task: even with sustained adult involvement, part of the hygiene routine remained unfinished. Consistent with her mother’s priority for personal care, Sofía needs to learn to start showering with fewer reminders and wash her hair independently.

In communication, Sofía’s ability to speak at length does not carry over to a reciprocal exchange. During direct observation at home, Sofía spoke about train schedules for 11 minutes without pausing and did not respond to 2 attempts to change the topic. The IEP describes similar difficulty taking conversational turns at school, and the CDE notes that Sofía does not clarify what she means when misunderstood. Sofía needs to recognize another person’s contribution, respond to it and clarify her message so that both people can take part.

Difficulty coping with demands interferes with attendance. Her mother reported school refusal on 6 of 20 school days: Sofía cried, locked herself in the bathroom or would not board the bus. Her mother reported arriving late to work or relying on her grandmother to keep Sofía home on those days. The IEP also documented departures from class 2 to 4 times per week, usually during writing or group work. These patterns support the BCBA’s finding that Leaving the area and school refusal is maintained by escape from academic and social demands. Verbal outbursts, Property destruction and Hand biting (self-injury) are additional targets. Sofía needs to learn to request help or a break, manage changes and resume demands so she can leave for school and participate in instruction.

Physical aggression places Sofía’s brother at risk. Her mother reported that Sofía hits, kicks or pushes him several times a day, often over the tablet or remote, and described a bruise on his upper arm. Direct observation documented 6 episodes in 6 hours across home and community routines; the IEP also reported physical altercations with peers about 2 times per week. The BCBA identified escape from demands as the primary maintaining consequence and access to preferred items as secondary. In the caregiver interview, her mother described homework being dropped and the tablet being given when behavior escalates. To protect her brother and participate safely with peers, Sofía needs ways to manage demands and conflicts over preferred items without physical contact.

Difficulty joining peers limits Sofía’s participation even when another child initiates play. During direct observation at the park, 2 girls invited Sofía to play tag. She responded with a bus schedule rather than answering the invitation. The girls walked away, and Sofía played alone on the climbing structure. The evaluating psychologist also documented solitary play during free time at the school summer program. To pursue the friendship her mother wants for her, Sofía needs to recognize an invitation, respond to the peer and join the shared activity.

Direct observation showed where adult assistance did not resolve the difficulty. At home, neither of 2 homework attempts ended in completed work. At the library, Sofía sat on the floor and screamed for 9 minutes when asked to leave, until a staff member asked her mother to take her outside. On the way to the park, Sofía pulled free of her mother’s hand and crossed the street without looking. Although no cars were present, the crossing showed why staying with an adult and checking for traffic require direct teaching during outings. District approval for BCBA observation at school remained pending; school findings came from the IEP and the evaluating psychologist’s summer program observation.

These findings establish the medical necessity of individualized ABA at home, where hygiene, homework and school departure break down, and in the community, where transitions, street crossings and peer play are impaired. Teaching will match skills to what maintains each behavior. Caregiver training will help her mother and grandmother support independent responses during these routines. Her mother’s BASC-3 PRQ responses indicated concerns with discipline practices, parenting confidence and relational frustration, consistent with her report that she has begun avoiding outings. Home and community practice complements the IEP’s specialized instruction, pragmatic speech-language therapy and counseling without duplicating classroom instruction or school goals. It addresses daily behavior and independence rather than the medication management provided by psychiatry. Progress will be measured through direct data on target behaviors, prompts needed for hygiene, independent responses to demands and participation in community activities, with the Vineland-3 and BASC-3 PRQ repeated at reassessment.

The BCBA’s plan will use the same discriminative stimulus (SD) for each skill or replacement behavior when Sofía first learns it and when she practices it with other people and in other settings. For example, Sofía will practice requesting help or a break during homework with both her mother and her grandmother, rather than only with the adult who first teaches the skill. For conversational turn-taking, Sofía will practice responding to her brother’s topic at home and to a peer’s topic at the neighborhood park. At school, her Individual Education Plan (IEP) provides opportunities to use her break card during class with her teacher and to take conversational turns during structured peer activities. These school routines provide opportunities for carryover from home and community treatment. The BCBA will adjust the prompt hierarchy as Sofía responds more independently across people and routines.

After Sofía masters each skill, the BCBA will use weekly probes to check whether she continues to perform it independently. The BCBA will thin reinforcement from continuous to intermittent and fade prompts as Sofía maintains the skill. If performance drops, the BCBA will reinstate the previous reinforcement schedule and the prompts that were removed. Once Sofía regains her prior level of performance, the BCBA will thin reinforcement and fade those prompts again.

During the caregiver interview, Sofía’s mother reported that homework is sometimes set aside or Sofía receives the tablet when behavior escalates. These consequences can maintain behavior during demands and compete with learning to request help or a break. During direct observation at home, Sofía entered the shower only after repeated verbal prompts. Continued reliance on reminders could limit independent bathing. Her mother also reported avoiding outings, which reduces opportunities to practice safe street crossing.

Leaving the area and school refusal exposes Sofía to traffic. During direct observation on the way to the park, she pulled free of her mother’s hand once and ran across the street without looking; no cars were present. Her Individual Education Plan (IEP) documented classroom departures 2 to 4 times per week, interrupting instruction. Her mother reported refusal on 6 of 20 school days, resulting in missed school or her mother arriving late to work. Her mother reported Physical aggression toward Sofía’s brother several times daily, including an upper-arm bruise. The IEP documented pushing or kicking peers about 2 times per week. During a follow-up call, her mother described Sofía threatening to kill her brother while holding a butter knife. She put it down when her grandmother directed her to; no one was hurt.

Direct observation documented Hand biting (self-injury) 3 times during homework and bedtime, with red marks but no broken skin. Separately, her mother reported that head banging caused a cut above Sofía’s eyebrow that required urgent care; no treatment record was available. Direct observation documented 3 episodes of Property destruction at home. At school, the IEP described a thrown chair that prompted a classroom evacuation. Across home and community observations, 6 Verbal outbursts lasted 6 to 15 minutes and disrupted homework, evening routines and departure from the library. Her mother reported more pronounced afternoon outbursts since Sofía began methylphenidate.

During the follow-up call, her mother reported that the caregivers remove her brother from the area, stop talking to Sofía, move breakable objects and wait for the behavior to end. The BCBA will retain these family strategies where possible and use least-restrictive, function-based procedures. The Crisis Plan addresses responses to dangerous behavior.
